title: The Lewis and Clark Expedition
intro: After the Louisiana Purchase, President Thomas Jefferson commissioned the Corps of Discovery under Captain Meriwether Lewis and Second Lieutenant William Clark. It was to find a practical water route across the continent, map the land and establish relations with the Native American nations along the Missouri River.
ending: The Corps reached St. Louis on 23 September 1806. It had reached the Pacific but found no continuous waterway to it, and it had relied on the help of about two dozen Native American nations. The expedition also served to assert American sovereignty over lands those nations already inhabited.

stops.text: Under Clark's command the Corps set out at 4 pm up the Missouri in a keelboat and two pirogues. It may have had as many as 45 members, among them York, a Black man enslaved by Clark.
stops.quote: The Corps of Discovery departed from Camp Dubois (Camp Wood) at 4 pm on May 14, 1804.

stops.text: Lewis joined the party at St. Charles, Missouri, six days after it left Camp Dubois. The expedition set out again the next afternoon, 21 May, and followed the Missouri upriver.
stops.quote: Under Clark's command, they traveled up the Missouri River in their keelboat and two pirogues to St. Charles, Missouri, where Lewis joined them six days later. The expedition set out the next afternoon, May 21.

stops.text: Sergeant Charles Floyd died, apparently of acute appendicitis, the only member of the expedition to die. He was buried on a bluff by the river with a cedar post carrying his name and the day of his death.
stops.quote: On August 20, 1804, Sergeant Charles Floyd died, apparently from acute appendicitis.

stops.place: The Bad River, near Fort Pierre
stops.text: The expedition met the Lakota, whom it called Sioux, under chiefs including Black Buffalo and the Partisan. The chiefs demanded tribute for passage, warriors seized a boat, and Lewis and Clark made a show of force until Black Buffalo ordered his men back.
stops.quote: However, there was a tense confrontation on September 25, 1804, with the Teton-Sioux tribe (also known as the Lakota people, one of the three tribes that comprise the Great Sioux Nation), under chiefs that included Black Buffalo and the Partisan.

stops.text: The party wintered in the Mandan nation's territory, where it met the trapper Toussaint Charbonneau and his young Shoshone wife Sacagawea. Peace with the Mandan chiefs was made by sharing a ceremonial pipe, and the keelboat went back to St. Louis on 7 April 1805.
stops.quote: In the winter of 1804–1805, the party built Fort Mandan, near present-day Washburn, North Dakota.

legs.title: Over the mountains to the Pacific

stops.text: Sacagawea became dangerously ill at the Marias River. She found relief by drinking mineral water from the sulphur spring that fed into it.
stops.quote: When the expedition reached the Marias River, on June 16, 1805, Sacagawea became dangerously ill. She was able to find relief by drinking mineral water from the sulphur spring that fed into the river.

stops.text: The expedition followed the Missouri to its headwaters and crossed the Continental Divide near Lemhi Pass. Lewis and Clark held a mistaken belief that boats could easily be carried from the Missouri's headwaters to the Columbia.
stops.quote: The expedition crossed the Continental Divide of the Americas near the Lemhi Pass, eventually coming to the Columbia River, and the Pacific Ocean in 1805.

stops.text: The party went north to Traveler's Rest and crossed the Bitterroot Mountains at Lolo Pass, then came down on foot to the Clearwater River.
stops.quote: They followed the Missouri to its headwaters, and over the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass, then north to Traveler's Rest, and crossed the Bitteroots at Lolo Pass. They descended on foot, then proceeded in canoes down the Clearwater, Snake, and Columbia rivers

stops.text: The party went down the Clearwater, Snake and Columbia rivers in canoes, past Celilo Falls and what is now Portland. The sight of Mount Hood showed that they had almost reached the Pacific.
stops.quote: They descended on foot, then proceeded in canoes down the Clearwater, Snake, and Columbia rivers, past Celilo Falls and present-day Portland, at the confluence of the Willamette and Columbia rivers.

stops.text: The expedition sighted the Pacific Ocean on 7 November 1805. It then camped in a storm-wracked place Clark called Dismal Nitch, short of food because the elk had retreated and the party had too little to buy from neighbouring peoples.
stops.quote: The expedition sighted the Pacific Ocean for the first time on November 7, 1805, arriving two weeks later. The expedition faced the beginning of its second bitter winter camped on the north side of the Columbia River, in a storm-wracked area Clark called Dismal Nitch.

stops.text: The majority voted to move camp to the south side of the Columbia, and Sacagawea and York took part in the vote. The party built Fort Clatsop on the Netul River and spent the winter there, many of the men ill with colds and influenza.
stops.quote: On November 24, 1805, the majority of the party voted to move their camp to the south side of the Columbia River near modern Astoria, Oregon. Both Sacagawea and the enslaved York participated in the vote.

stops.text: The journey home began on 23 March 1806, first by canoe up the Columbia and later overland. Before leaving, Clark gave the Chinook a letter for the next ship captain to call, Captain Hill, which reached Jefferson before the Corps did.
stops.quote: By March 22, the stormy weather had subsided and the following morning, on March 23, 1806, the journey home began.

stops.text: At Camp Chopunnish on the Clearwater the party gathered 65 horses but could not cross the snowbound Bitterroot Mountains. When Native Americans stole Lewis's dog Seaman, he warned the chief that further wrongdoing would mean instant death.
stops.quote: They made their way to Camp Chopunnish in Idaho, along the north bank of the Clearwater River, where the members of the expedition collected 65 horses in preparation to cross the Bitterroot Mountains, lying between modern-day Idaho and western Montana. However, the range was still covered in snow, which prevented the expedition from making the crossing.

stops.text: The Corps split in two so Lewis could explore the Marias. His group of four met Blackfeet men, who tried to steal their weapons in the night, and the soldiers killed two of them. Lewis and three others fled over 100 miles in a day.
stops.quote: On July 3, before crossing the Continental Divide, the Corps split into two teams so Lewis could explore the Marias River. Lewis's group of four met some men from the Blackfeet nation. During the night, the Blackfeet tried to steal their weapons. In the struggle, the soldiers killed two Blackfeet men.

stops.place: Confluence of the Yellowstone and Missouri
stops.text: The two groups met again. Clark had passed through Crow territory, where half his horses vanished in the night. As they reunited, the hunter Pierre Cruzatte mistook Lewis for an elk and shot him in the thigh.
stops.quote: Lewis and Clark stayed separated until they reached the confluence of the Yellowstone and Missouri Rivers on August 11. As the groups reunited, one of Clark's hunters, Pierre Cruzatte, mistook Lewis for an elk and fired, injuring Lewis in the thigh.

stops.text: The Corps returned quickly down the Missouri and reached St. Louis on 23 September 1806. It then reported its findings to Jefferson through maps, sketches and various journals.
stops.quote: They reached St. Louis on September 23, 1806.

notes: The article uses 'sea' or 'land' only loosely: the journey was on rivers, so all stops are marked 'land'. Years for Lemhi Pass, Lolo Pass and Celilo Falls are 1805 by inference (the article gives only the sequence and the Pacific sighting in 1805); Camp Chopunnish's April 1806 is likewise inferred from the return beginning in March 1806. The article's Lakota confrontation is told twice, with slightly different details (the Partisan taking an oar; Black Buffalo persuading Lewis to hand out tobacco); I followed the second. Left out: Pittsburgh and Louisville in 1803 (the article gives 1803 for the start but the departure it dates is Camp Dubois), Kansas City and Omaha (named in passing), Travelers' Rest as its own stop, Mount Hood, the feints and other places named without events. The last stop's text mentions the maps; the article gives the figure of about 140 maps in another section. Check wp titles 'Camp Dubois' and 'Dismal Nitch' (may be redirects) and 'Clearwater River (Idaho)'. Sacagawea's and York's accounts: the article notes much about Sacagawea is exaggeration or fiction and does not name her as guide, so the texts do not call her one.
